title: Is there a worst way to die?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether there is a worst way to die, drawing on a recent story about a tea vendor in India who set himself on fire. They cover polls on the worst way to die (immolation and drowning rank high; dying alone and lack of pain relief also come up), a Gallup poll showing few people fear death, a plane crash thought experiment, and Ernest Becker's theory that culture distracts us from mortality. They also discuss the shift from home deaths and sitting up with the dead to modern life expectancy and life support, bereavement photography, Walter Schels' "Life Before Death" photo series, and a teaser for an article on the Missiplicity pet cloning project. Ads for Visa and the camera are read during the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and India self-immolation story
segments.summary: Hosts open with a Visa ad read, then Josh recounts a tea vendor in India who set himself on fire after being abused by a local government official, and says it reminded him of his article on the worst way to die.

segments.title: Research on the worst way to die
segments.summary: Josh explains there is no objective measure of the worst death. He says Gallup had no poll on it, and a Gallup poll found only a small share of people afraid to die. Immolation and drowning usually rank highest in informal polls, and a British poll found dying alone was a common answer.

segments.title: Dying alone and lack of pain relief
segments.summary: The hosts discuss dying alone, citing Isaac Hayes and Elvis Presley as examples. Lack of pain relief came second in the poll responses. Reframing as the best way to die, they suggest dying in your sleep.

segments.title: Plane crash as a worst death
segments.summary: Chuck names a plane crash as his worst death, noting the minutes of awareness during a fall and the panic of passengers. Josh jokes that a Gallup poll on a falling plane would show higher fear.

segments.title: Ernest Becker and the denial of death
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Ernest Becker's psychology of death, arguing culture distracts people from mortality and that the unconscious mind then seeks outlets such as violence or war. Becker died at 49 of cancer.

segments.title: Death at home, life expectancy and life support
segments.summary: The hosts describe how open-casket and home wakes have declined and how people once sat up with the dead. Average life expectancy rose from about 49 in 1900 to nearly 78 in 2008, and machines now prolong life, which they see as further denial of death.

segments.title: Bereavement and post-mortem photography
segments.summary: The hosts discuss 19th-century post-mortem photos, including Jesse James's casket viewing, and modern bereavement photography used by parents of stillborn or very young children. They also mention famous morbid photos of Pablo Escobar and Lizzie Borden's father.

segments.title: Walter Schels' Life Before Death series
segments.summary: Josh describes German photographer Walter Schels' Life Before Death series, which pairs portraits of terminally ill people taken before and after death. The Guardian ran a feature on it, and the hosts debate whether it is uplifting or depressing.

segments.title: Visa ad and Missiplicity teaser
segments.summary: A Visa ad read, then the hosts tease an article on the Missiplicity project about cloning pets, and Chuck says it unsettles him.
